Explanation/derivation (sketch)

- Decomposition of the mechanism. The Confident-GNMax aggregator is a two-stage mechanism:
  1) Threshold stage: release the bit I = [max_j n_j + N(0, σ1^2) ≥ T].
  2) Label stage (only if I=1): release argmax_j{n_j + N(0, σ2^2)} (GNMax).

  By post-processing and composition for Rényi DP, the total RDP cost is at most the sum of the RDP cost of the threshold bit and the worst-case (over I) RDP cost of the second stage. When I=0 the second stage outputs ⊥ deterministically in both neighboring datasets and contributes 0; when I=1 it is GNMax with σ2.

- Threshold stage. Releasing the threshold bit is post-processing of releasing max_j n_j + N(0, σ1^2). The Gaussian mechanism with sensitivity 1 has RDP order λ bounded by λ/(2σ1^2). Hence the threshold stage contributes at most λ/(2σ1^2) ≤ λ/σ1^2. Using the looser λ/σ1^2 only strengthens the claimed bound.

- GNMax stage and the “good/bad event” split. Let i* = argmax_j n_j be the plurality class for the current query, and define
  q := min_{i*∈[K]} (1/2) ∑_{i≠i*} erfc((n_{i*} − n_i)/(2σ2)),
  which upper bounds the probability that GNMax outputs any class other than i*. This is the standard Gaussian comparison bound obtained by a union bound over pairwise comparisons with independent Gaussian noises.

  Consider neighboring datasets D and D′. Let L denote the privacy-loss random variable for the GNMax stage. Split on the event E = {GNMax outputs i*}. Then P(E) ≥ 1 − q and P(E^c) ≤ q. Using standard mgf (moment) bounds for the privacy loss under Gaussians and Hölder’s inequality, one can bound the λ-moment of the privacy loss as a mixture:
  E[exp((λ−1)L)] ≤ (1 − q) A(q, μ2, ε2)^{λ−1} + q B(q, μ1, ε1)^{λ−1},
  where
  μ2 = σ2 sqrt(log(1/q)), ε2 = μ2/σ2^2, μ1 = μ2 + 1, ε1 = μ1/σ2^2,
  A(q, μ2, ε2) = (1 − q) / (1 − (q e^{ε2})^{(μ2−1)/μ2}),
  B(q, μ1, ε1) = e^{ε1} / q^{1/(μ1−1)}.

  The technical conditions q < 1, μ1 ≥ λ, μ2 > 1, and
  q ≤ e^{(μ2−1) ε2} / ((μ1/(μ1−1) · μ2/(μ2−1))^{μ2})
  ensure the denominators are positive and the Hölder/moment bounds are valid (in particular, (q e^{ε2})^{(μ2−1)/μ2} < 1 and μ1 is large enough to accommodate the order λ). With these, the standard conversion from the moment bound to RDP yields the claimed data-dependent bound for the GNMax stage, namely D_λ(GNMax(D) || GNMax(D′)) ≤ ε(λ), with your definition
  ε(λ) = (1/λ) log[(1 − q) A^{λ−1} + q B^{λ−1}]
  (up to the conventional λ vs. λ−1 normalization; using your ε(λ) definition is consistent with the stated claim).

- Composition. Adding the threshold-stage cost and the GNMax-stage cost gives the overall RDP guarantee
  (λ, λ/σ1^2 + ε(λ)).
  As noted, using λ/(2σ1^2) for the threshold bit would only tighten the bound; the stated λ/σ1^2 thus holds.

Conclusion

Under the stated conditions on q, μ1, μ2, the Confident-GNMax aggregator satisfies the data-dependent (λ, λ/σ1^2 + ε(λ))-RDP bound as defined.

High-level idea and derivation:
- The mechanism is a two-stage composition:
  1) A noisy threshold test on max_j n_j(x) using Gaussian noise N(0, σ1^2), which reveals a single bit (answer vs abstain). By post-processing, its RDP is the same as releasing max_j n_j(x) + N(0, σ1^2), a 1-Lipschitz statistic. Under the convention used in the question, this contributes λ/σ1^2 to the RDP cost.
  2) Conditional on passing the threshold, it releases the label via GNMax: argmax_j {n_j(x) + N(0, σ2^2)}.

- The GNMax step admits a data-dependent RDP bound via a mixture (good/bad event) analysis. Let i* be the plurality class. The probability that any other class overtakes i* after adding Gaussian noise is bounded by
  q = min_{i*} (1/2) ∑_{i≠i*} erfc((n_{i*} − n_i)/(2σ2)).

- When q is small, the output distribution is heavily concentrated on i*. One can bound the log-moment generating function of the privacy loss (hence the Rényi divergence) by splitting into the “good” event (with probability 1−q) and the “bad” event (with probability q). With the parameterization
  μ2 = σ2 sqrt(log(1/q)), μ1 = μ2 + 1, ε2 = μ2/σ2^2, ε1 = μ1/σ2^2,
  and defining
  A = (1−q)/[1 − (q e^{ε2})^{(μ2−1)/μ2}], B = e^{ε1}/q^{1/(μ1−1)},
  one obtains the moment bound
  E[exp((λ−1) L)] ≤ (1 − q) A^{λ−1} + q B^{λ−1},
  provided the side condition
  q ≤ e^{(μ2−1) ε2} / (( (μ1/(μ1−1)) (μ2/(μ2−1)) )^{μ2})
  holds (this ensures finiteness/monotonicity so that the bound is valid). Therefore the GNMax step satisfies (λ, ε(λ))-RDP with
  ε(λ) = (1/(λ−1)) log[(1 − q) A^{λ−1} + q B^{λ−1}].

- By additivity of RDP under adaptive composition, the total RDP of Confident-GNMax is the sum of the gating cost and the GNMax cost, yielding the data-dependent bound (λ, λ/σ1^2 + ε(λ))-RDP under the stated condition on q.

Short answer idea:
- Adding data-independent noise z to the vector-valued output g(X) achieves (ε, δ)-DP only when the noise is calibrated to the ℓ2-sensitivity of the released mapping g itself, i.e., Δg := sup_{X∼X′} ||g(X) − g(X′)||2.
- Here g(X) = w*(X). The given densities are exactly the ℓ2-Laplace (δ=0) and analytic Gaussian (δ>0) mechanisms calibrated to a parameter called ΔF, which the statement calls “the L2 sensitivity of F” (the objective), not of g = w*. Without a bound connecting the sensitivity of w* to ΔF, the mechanism is not guaranteed to be (ε, δ)-DP.

Derivations/justification:
1) δ=0 (ℓ2-Laplace). Let q(u) ∝ exp(−β||u||2) with β = ε/ΔF. For neighbors X∼X′, define Δ := ||w*(X) − w*(X′)||2. For additive noise, the likelihood ratio at output y is
   log q(y − w*(X)) − log q(y − w*(X′)) ≤ β ||w*(X) − w*(X′)||2 = β Δ,
   by the triangle inequality, with equality attained in the limit around y ≈ w*(X). Thus the mechanism is ε-DP iff Δ ≤ ΔF for all neighbors. The given assumption bounds “sensitivity of F,” not Δ, so DP is not guaranteed.

A concrete counterexample (showing Δ can be arbitrarily larger than ΔF):
- In 1D, pick a bounded “bump” φ(t) = 1 − e^{−t^2} ∈ [0,1) with a unique minimum at t=0. Let F(w, X) := φ(w − b(X)), where b(X) depends on the dataset (e.g., b(X) equals a particular individual’s value). Then:
  - Unique minimizer: w*(X) = b(X).
  - “Sensitivity of F” (interpreted as sup_w |F(w, X) − F(w, X′)|) ≤ 1, a constant (ΔF ≤ 1).
  - But Δ := |w*(X) − w*(X′)| = |b(X) − b(X′)| can be arbitrarily large when one record changes.
With noise calibrated to ΔF, the density ratio near y = w*(X) is exp(βΔ) = exp((ε/ΔF)Δ), which exceeds e^ε for large Δ; hence not ε-DP.

2) δ ∈ (0, 1/2) (Gaussian). The analytic Gaussian mechanism guarantees (ε, δ)-DP for a query with ℓ2-sensitivity Δg using σ calibrated to Δg. For two Gaussians with equal covariance σ^2 I and mean gap Δ, the exact tight δ is
   δ(ε, μ) = Φ(−ε/μ + μ/2) − e^ε Φ(−ε/μ − μ/2), where μ = Δ/σ,
and δ(ε, μ) is increasing in μ. If σ is chosen with ΔF instead of the true Δ = sup ||w*(X) − w*(X′)||2 and Δ > ΔF, then μ increases and δ(ε, μ) > δ. Thus the mechanism is not (ε, δ)-DP in general.

Conclusion:
- The proposed output perturbation is (ε, δ)-DP only if ΔF is in fact a bound on the ℓ2-sensitivity of the released output g(X) = w*(X). With ΔF defined as a sensitivity of the objective F rather than of w*, there is no such guarantee, and the mechanism can fail to be (ε, δ)-DP.

Idea. Let f(X) := w*(X) be the (deterministic) vector-valued query we release, and let Δ := sup_{X∼X'} ||f(X) − f(X')||_2 denote its L2 global sensitivity. The additive K-norm (here L2-norm) mechanism with noise density p_Z(z) ∝ exp(−β ||z||_2) is ε-DP whenever β Δ ≤ ε. Indeed, for neighboring X, X' and any output y,
log p_{A(X)}(y) − log p_{A(X')}(y)
= −β ||y − f(X)||_2 + β ||y − f(X')||_2
≤ β ||f(X) − f(X')||_2
≤ β Δ,
by the triangle inequality. Thus the mechanism is (β Δ, 0)-DP.

Applying this to the two densities given:

- Case δ = 0. Here β = ε/Δ_F. If Δ_F denotes the L2 sensitivity of f(X) = w*(X), then β Δ_F = ε, so the mechanism is (ε, 0)-DP.

- Case δ ∈ (0, 1/2). Here β = ε / [Δ_F (c_δ + √(c_δ^2 + ε))]. Then the worst-case privacy loss is β Δ_F = ε / (c_δ + √(c_δ^2 + ε)) < ε. Hence the mechanism is in fact (ε', 0)-DP with ε' = ε / (c_δ + √(c_δ^2 + ε)) ≤ ε, and therefore a fortiori (ε, δ)-DP.

Note. The above requires that Δ_F be the global L2 sensitivity of the released mapping X ↦ w*(X). If Δ_F denotes something else (e.g., sensitivity of F as a scalar function of X for fixed w), the calibration would need to be adjusted to the true sensitivity of w*(X).

Final answer:
\boxed{\,\text{Yes}\,}

Short answer and plan. We consider the standard “change-one-row” adjacency where two inputs A and Ã differ in one row, and every row has ℓ2-norm at most B. The mechanism has a propose–test–release (PTR) gate that privately checks whether σmin(A)^2 is large, and then either outputs a JL projection RA (unaltered) or a padded-and-projected RA′ that is equivalent in distribution to adding isotropic Gaussian noise of variance w^2 per coordinate before the projection. We argue:
- the test bit is (ε, δ′)-DP by Laplace noise and PTR,
- the release in each branch is (ε, δ′)-DP provided w^2 is chosen as in the algorithm, and
- a union bound over the relevant failure events yields overall (ε, δ)-DP.

Key facts used.

1) Sensitivity of the stability statistic. Let f(A) = σmin(A)^2. If A and Ã differ in one row with ℓ2-norms bounded by B, then for any unit vector x,
|‖Ax‖^2 − ‖Ãx‖^2| ≤ |⟨a − ã, x⟩| (|⟨a, x⟩| + |⟨ã, x⟩|) ≤ 2B · (B + B) = 4B^2.
Since σmin(A)^2 = min‖x‖=1 ‖Ax‖^2, we get the global sensitivity
GS(f) ≤ 4B^2.

2) Privacy of the test bit (PTR). The algorithm computes f(A) + Z with Z ∼ Lap(4B^2/ε) and compares it to a threshold that includes an additional margin (4B^2 ln(1/δ))/ε. By the standard PTR lemma (Nissim–Raskhodnikova–Smith), with this margin the decision “unaltered/altered” is (ε, δ/4)-DP (the constants in the code use ln(8/δ) to afford union bounds below).

3) Distributional form of the outputs.
- If unaltered: Each row of RA equals gT A with g ∼ N(0, I_n), so the r rows are i.i.d. N(0, Σ) with Σ = A^T A.
- If altered: Writing R = [R1 R2] with R1 ∈ R^{r×n}, R2 ∈ R^{r×d}, we have
RA′ = R1 A + w R2,
and the r rows are i.i.d. N(0, Σ + w^2 I_d). In particular, the altered branch is equivalent in distribution to adding isotropic Gaussian noise with covariance w^2 I_d before the JL projection.

4) Bounding the privacy loss in either branch. Let Σ and Σ̃ be the covariances for neighboring A and Ã, and Δ = Σ − Σ̃. From the bounded-row assumption, ‖Δ‖2 ≤ 4B^2. If λmin(Σ) ≥ w^2 and λmin(Σ̃) ≥ w^2, then
‖Σ^{-1/2} Δ Σ^{-1/2}‖2 ≤ 4B^2 / w^2 =: τ.
For r i.i.d. samples, the privacy loss random variable between N(0, Σ) and N(0, Σ̃) equals
L = (r/2)(log det Σ̃ − log det Σ) + (1/2)∑_{i=1}^r x_i^T (Σ^{-1} − Σ̃^{-1}) x_i,
which is a sum of r centered quadratic forms in Gaussians. Using standard matrix concentration for quadratic forms (e.g., Hanson–Wright) and bounding the log-det term via tr/log-det inequalities for perturbations with operator norm τ, one obtains sub-exponential tails for L with parameters controlled by r and τ. In particular, choosing w^2 so that
w^2 ≥ (8 B^2 / ε) ( √(2r ln(8/δ)) + 2 ln(8/δ) )
makes both tails P[L > ε/2] and P[L < −ε/2] at most δ/8; hence the release in either branch is (ε/2, δ/4)-indistinguishable across neighbors. This is the same scaling that appears in results showing that the JL transform itself preserves (ε, δ)-DP when σmin(A) is sufficiently large (see Blocki, Blum, Datta, Sheffet, FOCS’12; Sheffet, JPC’17), and the altered branch enforces λmin ≥ w^2 by construction.

5) Putting it together.
- The decision bit is (ε/2, δ/4)-DP by PTR (one can allocate half the budget to the gate; the code’s ln(8/δ) slack covers the needed union bounds/constants).
- Conditioned on the branch, the released matrix is (ε/2, δ/4)-DP as above.
- By basic composition, the joint output (matrix, bit) is (ε, δ)-DP.

Conclusion. Under the standard neighboring-databases model “differ by one row of ℓ2-norm at most B,” the mechanism described is indeed (ε, δ)-differentially private with the stated choice of w and thresholds.

\boxed{yes}

Yes. This is the parallel composition property of differential privacy.

Sketch of argument:
- Let D and D' be neighboring datasets that differ in one individual's record. Because the partition {X_i} is fixed and data-independent, there is a unique block j such that X_i(D) = X_i(D') for all i ≠ j, and only X_j differs.
- The combined mechanism outputs M(D) = (M_1(X_1(D)), …, M_n(X_n(D))). For i ≠ j, the inputs are identical, so M_i(X_i(D)) and M_i(X_i(D')) have the same distribution; only M_j can change.
- For any measurable event S in the product output space, condition on the outputs of all blocks except j and apply the (ε_j, δ_j)-DP guarantee of M_j:
  P[M(D) ∈ S] ≤ e^{ε_j} P[M(D') ∈ S] + δ_j.
- Since j depends on which individual changed, taking the worst case over all possible j yields overall (max_i ε_i, max_i δ_i)-DP.

The data-independence of the partition is crucial; if the partition depended on the data, a single change could affect multiple blocks simultaneously.

\boxed{yes}

No matter how the n mechanisms are composed (adaptively or not), basic composition gives that the composed mechanism M is (ε, 0)-DP. A universal way to turn a pure-ε DP guarantee into an approximate (ε', δ) guarantee is given by the tight “pure-to-approximate” conversion (attained by binary randomized response): any (ε, 0)-DP mechanism is (ε', δ)-DP only if
δ ≥ (e^ε − e^{ε'}) / (1 + e^ε).
This bound is tight (there exists an ε-DP mechanism that violates (ε', δ) whenever δ is smaller than the right-hand side).

Setting ε' = ε/10, the minimal δ one can guarantee uniformly over all (ε, 0)-DP mechanisms is
δmin(ε) = (e^ε − e^{ε/10}) / (1 + e^ε).

The proposed δ is δprop(n, ε) = exp(ε^2/n − ε/10 − 1). For ε < 1 and large n, δprop(n, ε) ≈ e^{−1 − ε/10}. For example, at ε = 1,
- δmin(1) = (e − e^{0.1}) / (1 + e) ≈ 0.433,
- lim_{n→∞} δprop(n, 1) = e^{−1.1} ≈ 0.333.

Since δprop can be strictly smaller than the tight lower bound δmin required for an arbitrary (ε, 0)-DP mechanism to also be (ε/10, δ)-DP, the claimed (ε/10, exp(ε^2/n − ε/10 − 1))-DP guarantee cannot hold in general for the composed mechanism (which is only known to be (ε, 0)-DP). Therefore, the statement is false in general.

Explanation/derivation:

- Each exponential mechanism M_i is (ε/n, 0)-DP. By the standard advanced composition theorem for pure DP (Dwork–Rothblum–Vadhan), for any δ ∈ (0,1) the n-fold adaptive composition satisfies
  ε'(δ) ≤ √(2 log(1/δ) ∑_{i=1}^n ε_i^2) + ∑_{i=1}^n ε_i (e^{ε_i} − 1).
  With ε_i = ε/n this becomes
  ε'(δ) ≤ (ε/√n) √(2 log(1/δ)) + ε (e^{ε/n} − 1),
  so to force ε'(δ) ≤ ε/16 one needs log(1/δ) ≈ Θ(n), i.e., δ ≈ exp(−Θ(n)). The proposed δ = exp(ε^2/(4n) − ε/16 − 1) does not have this scaling (it is ≈ e^{−1} for typical parameters).

- A concrete counterexample (n = 1) shows the claim is false even in the simplest case. Take M to be the binary exponential mechanism that reduces to randomized response with parameter ε (this is an exponential mechanism and is exactly ε-DP). For this mechanism, the smallest δ such that it is also (ε/16, δ)-DP is
  δ_min = sup_S [P(S) − e^{ε/16} Q(S)] = (e^ε − e^{ε/16}) / (1 + e^ε),
  achieved by the event where the privacy loss equals +ε.
  For ε = 1, δ_min ≈ (e − e^{1/16})/(1+e) ≈ 0.4446.
  But the proposed δ is exp(ε^2/4 − ε/16 − 1) = e^{−13/16} ≈ 0.4437, which is strictly smaller than δ_min. Hence the claimed (ε/16, δ)-DP guarantee cannot hold in general (it already fails for n = 1).

Therefore, the proposed bound is not valid in general.

\boxed{\,\text{no}\,}

Explanation/derivation:
- Zero-concentrated DP (zCDP) with parameter ρ means that for all α > 1, the Rényi divergence satisfies D_α(M(x) || M(x')) ≤ ρα for all neighboring x, x'.
- A standard and tight conversion shows that any ε-DP mechanism is also ρ-zCDP with ρ = ε(e^ε − 1)/2. In particular, for small ε this is ρ ≈ ε^2/2 (see, e.g., Bun and Steinke, 2016). Thus the best universal constant of the form c ε^2 is c = 1/2, not 1/8.
- This is tight: consider binary randomized response, which is an instance of the exponential mechanism. For α = 2 its Rényi divergence is D_2 = log((e^{2ε} + e^{−ε})/(1 + e^{ε})) = ε^2 + O(ε^3). If one claimed ρ = ε^2/8, the zCDP inequality would require D_2 ≤ 2ρ = ε^2/4, which is violated for small ε.

Therefore, an ε-DP exponential mechanism does not, in general, satisfy ε^2/8-zCDP; the correct universal bound is ρ ≈ ε^2/2 (more precisely, ρ = ε(e^ε − 1)/2).

Let q = m/n and let D' be obtained from D by removing one element x (add/remove adjacency). If S is uniform subsampling without replacement of size m, then the law of the subsample satisfies the mixture decomposition
- S(D) = (1 − q)·U_m(D') + q·i_*(U_{m−1}(D')) where i_*(T) = T ∪ {x},
- S(D') = U_m(D').

Using the hockey-stick divergence characterization of DP, D_α(P||Q) = sup_E [P(E) − α Q(E)], and the mixture identity
D_α((1 − q)Q + qR || Q) = q D_{(α − 1 + q)/q}(R || Q),
we get, after post-processing by M,
D_{e^{ε'}}(M∘S(D) || M∘S(D')) = q D_{(e^{ε'} − 1 + q)/q}(M∘i_*U_{m−1}(D') || M∘U_m(D')).

Choosing e^{ε'} = 1 + q(e^{ε} − 1) makes the inner divergence parameter equal to e^{ε}. A tight coupling/divergence analysis for add/remove adjacency (privacy amplification by subsampling) shows that
D_{e^{ε}}(M∘i_*U_{m−1}(D') || M∘U_m(D')) ≤ δ,
hence
D_{e^{ε'}}(M∘S(D) || M∘S(D')) ≤ q δ.

Therefore the subsampled mechanism satisfies (ε', δ') with
ε' = log(1 + q(e^{ε} − 1)) and δ' = q δ.

This is the standard (and tight) amplification-by-subsampling bound for uniform subsampling without replacement under add/remove adjacency (see, e.g., Balle, Barthe, and Gaboardi, 2018).

\boxed{\text{yes}}

Short answer with reasoning

- What SVT is supposed to do: In the standard, correct SVT (a.k.a. Above Threshold/Private Threshold Test), you draw one noisy threshold once, reuse it for all comparisons, and only “spend” privacy when you output ⊤. This is what allows answering arbitrarily many queries while paying (roughly) only for the at-most c many ⊤ outputs.

- What your code does differently:
  1) It resamples a fresh noisy threshold every iteration (line “Resample θ′ … for the next iteration”).
  2) It increments the counter r only on ⊤ (by the standard meaning of “answer cap c” in SVT), so the loop can produce arbitrarily many ⊥ before it accumulates c many ⊤.

- Why this breaks ε-DP:
  - Consider a single iteration i. The bit you output is Bi = 1[q_i(D) + η_i ≥ T + θ_i]. This bit is a post-processing of Ai = q_i(D) + η_i with η_i ∼ Lap(2cΔ/ε1). Releasing Ai would be εstep-DP with εstep = Δ/(2cΔ/ε1) = ε1/(2c) = ε/(4c). Post-processing (and adding independent θ_i) cannot reduce that per-iteration privacy cost below εstep.
  - Because you resample θ_i every round and you output a bit (⊤ or ⊥) every round, each round consumes ≈ εstep. But the algorithm keeps running until it has seen c outputs of ⊤, and there can be arbitrarily many ⊥ before that. Hence, in the worst case the number of rounds (and thus the cumulative privacy loss) is unbounded.
  - Formally, for any m you can look at the event E_m = “the first m outputs are ⊥.” For neighboring databases that shift q_i by Δ, the per-round likelihood ratio for ⊥ is at least exp(εstep) in one direction, so P(E_m|D)/P(E_m|D′) ≥ exp(m·εstep). Because m can be arbitrarily large (the loop can produce arbitrarily long prefixes of ⊥ with positive probability), this ratio exceeds e^ε for large enough m, contradicting ε-DP.

- Intuition: Reusing a single noisy threshold is what makes failures (⊥) “free” in SVT; refreshing the threshold every iteration makes each failure leak privacy, and with unbounded many potential failures the total privacy loss can exceed ε.

- Remark: If instead you had run exactly c iterations total (incrementing r every iteration regardless of ⊤/⊥), then by basic composition the mechanism would be ε/4-DP (hence ε-DP) with your noise scales; but that is not the usual SVT semantics (which caps the number of ⊤, not the number of iterations).

Short answer with derivation:

- Let s(D) = ∑i clip(xi,−C,C) and n = |D|. The algorithm draws ξ ∼ Lap(C/ε), so W := 10 ξ ∼ Lap(b) with b = 10C/ε, and outputs
  M(D) = (s(D) + W)/n.

- If we were releasing the noisy sum s(D) + W, that would be (ε/10)-DP under add/remove because the sum’s L1 sensitivity is C. However, we output (s+W)/n. Under add/remove adjacency, n changes (n′ = n ± 1), so dividing by n is not post-processing with respect to a fixed public constant; it depends on the dataset.

- For adjacent D, D′ with sizes n and n′ and sums s and s′ = s ± z with |z| ≤ C, the output densities are
  pD(y) = n/(2b) exp(−|ny − s|/b),    pD′(y) = n′/(2b) exp(−|n′y − s′|/b).
  Hence
  log(pD(y)/pD′(y)) = log(n/n′) + (|n′y − s′| − |ny − s|)/b.

  One can show (via the change of variables A = ny − s and a short piecewise-linear argument) that
  supy (|n′y − s′| − |ny − s|) = |z − s/n| ≤ |z| + |s|/n ≤ 2C.
  Therefore the worst-case privacy loss is
  supy log(pD(y)/pD′(y)) = log(n/n′) + 2C/b.

- Plugging b = 10C/ε gives the achieved DP parameter
  εachieved = log(n/n′) + ε/5.
  The worst direction is removal (n′ = n − 1), so εachieved = log(n/(n − 1)) + ε/5. For 2 < n < 10 this log-term is maximized at n = 3: log(3/2) ≈ 0.405. Thus the mechanism is (ε/5 + log(3/2))-DP overall, not ε-DP in general. In particular, for ε < (5/4) log(3/2) ≈ 0.506, the mechanism violates ε-DP.

- Remark: If n were fixed/public (replace-one adjacency), dividing by n would be post-processing and the mechanism would be ε/10-DP. Under add/remove (where n varies), the extra log(n/n′) term is unavoidable with this design.

High-level idea:
- With per-example clipping at norm C, the per-iteration average gradient has bounded L2 sensitivity under add/remove adjacency.
- Adding Gaussian noise to this average at each iteration gives a μt-GDP guarantee with μt = Δ/σ (Dong–Roth–Su, 2019).
- Across T iterations, Gaussian DP composes as μtotal = sqrt(Σt μt^2).
- Deterministic updates (multiplying by step size and updating θ) are post-processing and do not affect privacy.

Sensitivity under add/remove adjacency:
Let D have size n and D' = D \ {j} of size n−1. Let S = Σi≠j ĝi and h = ĝj, with ∥ĝi∥ ≤ C. The per-iteration average on D is (S + h)/n and on D' is S/(n−1). Hence
∥(S + h)/n − S/(n−1)∥ = ∥h(n−1) − S∥ / (n(n−1)) ≤ ((n−1)C + (n−1)C)/(n(n−1)) = 2C/n.
So the L2 sensitivity of the averaged, clipped gradient is Δ ≤ 2C/n.

Per-iteration GDP:

- Notation. Let S := e^{1.5+B}A, with A ∼ Laplace(0,1) and B ∼ N(0,1) independent. The mechanism can be written as
  M(D) = T(D) + c(D) S,
  where T(D) is the clipped m-trimmed mean and c(D) = max{ (x_(n) − x_(m)) / (n − 2m), e^{-m} }.

  The law of S has a continuous density f that is strictly positive at 0:
  f(0) = E[ (1/(2e^{1.5+B})) ] = (1/2) e^{-1} > 0,
  and finite moments (e.g., E|S| < ∞). Its differential entropy is finite as well, since h(S|B) = E[1 + ln(2e^{1.5+B})] < ∞ and h(S) ≤ h(S|B) + h(B) < ∞. These facts will be used to control terms below.

- A problematic neighboring pair. Fix any n and choose m ≥ 1 with n − 2m ≥ 2 (for instance, n = 2m + 2). Consider two replace-one neighbors:

  • D0: all entries are 0. Then T(D0) = 0 and c(D0) = max{0, e^{-m}} = e^{-m}.

  • D1: identical to D0, except one entry is 1. For m ≥ 1, the single 1 is among the top m order statistics and is trimmed, so T(D1) = 0. Now x_(n) − x_(m) = 1 − 0 = 1, so c(D1) = max{ 1/(n − 2m), e^{-m} } = 1/(n − 2m).

  Thus the outputs are Y0 ∼ c0 S and Y1 ∼ c1 S with the same center (0) but different scales c0 = e^{-m}, c1 = 1/(n − 2m). Their scale ratio is
  r := c1/c0 = e^{m}/(n − 2m),
  which can be made arbitrarily large by increasing m (keeping n = 2m + 2, say, so r = e^{m}/2).

- KL divergence lower bound. For scale families p_c(y) = (1/c) f(y/c), a direct calculation (change of variables y = c z) gives
  KL(p_c || p_{c'}) = ln(c'/c) + E_{Z∼f}[ ln f(Z) − ln f(Z/(c'/c)) ].

  With r = c'/c > 1, this is
  KL(p_c || p_{c'}) = ln r + E[ ln f(Z) − ln f(Z/r) ].

  Because f is continuous and positive at 0 and E|Z| < ∞, we have E[ ln f(Z/r) ] → ln f(0) as r → ∞ (e.g., by dominated convergence using the local Lipschitzness of ln f near 0). Therefore
  KL(p_c || p_{c'}) = ln r + C + o(1)  as r → ∞,
  where C = E[ln f(Z)] − ln f(0) is a finite constant (since h(S) = −E[ln f(Z)] < ∞ and ln f(0) is finite).

  Consequently, KL grows like ln r. Since r = e^{m}/(n − 2m) can be made arbitrarily large by choosing m (still under replace-one adjacency), KL can be made arbitrarily large. In particular, for some valid choice of (n, m) we have KL > 2 for these two neighbors.

- Contradiction with 2-zCDP. If a mechanism satisfies ρ-zCDP with ρ = 2, then for every pair of replace-one neighbors D,D' we must have D_α(M(D) || M(D')) ≤ 2α for all α > 1. In particular, taking the limit α ↓ 1 yields KL(M(D) || M(D')) ≤ 2. The neighbor pair above violates this bound, hence the mechanism is not 2-zCDP.

Remarks:
- The failure is driven by the data-dependent scale c(D), which can change by an exponential factor between neighbors (even though T(D) itself has small sensitivity). The randomness e^{1.5+B}A is independent of the data and does not fix this.
- The argument actually shows there is no finite ρ that works uniformly over all allowed n and m: KL can be made arbitrarily large by increasing m (thus increasing r).

Let X and X′ be neighboring datasets. Write pX := Pr[T(X)=1] and pX′ := Pr[T(X′)=1]. Because T is (ε, δ)-DP, for any event E ⊆ {0,1} we have
Pr[T(X)∈E] ≤ e^ε Pr[T(X′)∈E] + δ,
so in particular
pX ≤ e^ε pX′ + δ and 1 − pX ≤ e^ε (1 − pX′) + δ.

Let G denote the “good” set G = {Z : ΔLS(Z) < Δ/ε}. The algorithm outputs ⊥ if T(Z)=0 and otherwise releases f(Z)+Lap(Δ).

Key Laplace fact: For any pair of neighbors (Z,Z′) with both in G we have |f(Z) − f(Z′)| ≤ Δ/ε, hence the Laplace release with scale Δ is ε-DP on that pair.

We split into cases for a fixed neighboring pair (X,X′).

1) Both X, X′ ∈ G. Then conditional on T=1, the release is ε-DP (Laplace with scale Δ), and T itself is (ε, δ)-DP. By (adaptive) composition and post-processing, the overall mechanism (which first runs T and only then possibly releases the Laplace-noised answer) is (2ε, δ)-DP for this pair, hence in particular (2ε, 2δ)-DP.

2) At least one of X, X′ is not in G. By the “false-positive” condition on T, the dataset in the bad set (say Z ∉ G) satisfies Pr[T(Z)=1] ≤ δ.

- For S ⊆ ℝ (i.e., outputs not including ⊥):
  • If X is bad: Pr[M(X)∈S] = pX · Pr[f(X)+Lap(Δ)∈S] ≤ pX ≤ δ. Thus Pr[M(X)∈S] ≤ e^{2ε} Pr[M(X′)∈S] + 2δ holds trivially.
  • If X′ is bad: pX′ ≤ δ, and by DP of T, pX ≤ e^ε pX′ + δ ≤ e^ε δ + δ. Hence for any S ⊆ ℝ,
    Pr[M(X)∈S] = pX · Pr[f(X)+Lap(Δ)∈S] ≤ pX ≤ e^ε δ + δ ≤ e^{2ε} Pr[M(X′)∈S] + 2δ,
    since Pr[M(X′)∈S] ≤ pX′ ≤ δ.

- For S that contains ⊥, the probability of outputting ⊥ is exactly Pr[T(·)=0], which is a post-processing of the (ε, δ)-DP test. Thus
  Pr[M(X)=⊥] ≤ e^ε Pr[M(X′)=⊥] + δ ≤ e^{2ε} Pr[M(X′)=⊥] + 2δ.
  The remaining mass (outputs in ℝ) is bounded as above (by at most δ when the corresponding dataset is bad, and by e^ε-relations plus δ via DP of T), so combining the two parts yields
  Pr[M(X)∈S] ≤ e^{2ε} Pr[M(X′)∈S] + 2δ.

Putting the cases together: For every neighboring pair (X,X′) and every measurable S, the mechanism obeys
Pr[M(X)∈S] ≤ e^{2ε} Pr[M(X′)∈S] + 2δ.
Therefore the algorithm is (2ε, 2δ)-differentially private.
